topic: The forgetting curve, retrieval practice and spacing, applied to workplace training
scope_note: Conservative, textbook-level claims only. No percentages of forgetting; shapes and directions instead.

facts.statement: Hermann Ebbinghaus measured his own memory by learning lists of nonsense syllables and testing how much he kept over time, and published the work in 1885.
facts.reference_hint: Ebbinghaus (1885), Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology

facts.statement: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning and slows down over time, so retention drawn on a graph drops steeply at first and then levels off; this shape is called the forgetting curve.
facts.reference_hint: Ebbinghaus (1885); many replications, e.g. Murre and Dros (2015)

facts.statement: How fast a person forgets depends on the material, how meaningful it is to them and what they already know, so no single forgetting percentage applies to everyone.
Retrieval practice, actively recalling information for example by testing yourself, leads to better long-term retention than spending the same time rereading it.
Rereading tends to feel effective because the material becomes familiar and easy to process, and that familiarity is easily mistaken for being able to recall it.
facts.caveat: a well supported explanation of why learners prefer rereading; the size of the effect varies

facts.statement: Practice spread out over time with gaps leads to better long-term retention than the same amount of practice crammed together; this is called the spacing effect.
Cramming can support performance shortly afterwards, but what was crammed is forgotten faster than what was studied with spacing.
Each successful recall makes a memory more durable, so later reviews can come after longer gaps than earlier ones.
facts.caveat: the best gaps depend on how long the knowledge must last; there is no universal schedule

facts.statement: A practical guideline for training is a first self-test within about a day, another a few days later, and another about a week or two after that.
facts.caveat: a guideline, not a rule; stretch the gaps when recall is easy and shorten them when it fails
facts.reference_hint: common application of spacing research in workplace learning

facts.statement: Retrieval practice does not need to be long: recalling the key points from memory for a few minutes and then checking them against the notes counts.
Checking your answer after trying to recall it matters, because feedback corrects mistakes and strengthens what was right.
facts.caveat: feedback should come soon after the attempt

not_claimed: that people forget a fixed percentage of training within a day or a week
learning styles or matching teaching to visual, auditory or kinaesthetic learners
the learning pyramid or cone of experience retention percentages
that brain training games improve memory in general
exact optimal review intervals for everyone
